Marxism-Leninism aims at state or collective ownership of the means of production as the basis of socialism.
Private ownership of nearly all productive assets is the capitalism that Marxism-Leninism exists to abolish.
Every Trotskyist current wants the means of production owned collectively in a workers' state.
Trotskyism treats private ownership of productive assets as the capitalist order that revolution must abolish.
Trotskyists of every variant want an economy that is democratically and centrally planned, not run by market competition.
Trotskyism is defined by internationalism and permanent revolution, and it rejects putting national loyalty above the international working class.
Democratic socialism defines itself against one-party rule and requires competitive elections.
Democratic socialists hold that free party competition and peaceful transfer of power are part of socialism itself.
Democratic socialism wants the major means of production socially owned, so mostly private ownership contradicts its aim.
Social ownership of large enterprises by the public, cooperatives or workers is the core economic goal of democratic socialism.
Market socialism is defined by worker or social ownership of firms in place of private capital.
Private shareholder ownership of large firms is exactly the capitalist ownership that market socialism replaces.
Market socialism requires productive capital to be socially or worker-owned, not mostly in private hands.
Market socialism, by definition, keeps prices and markets rather than central planning to coordinate production.
Eco-socialism calls for common ownership of energy, land and key industries, and sees private accumulation as the driver of ecological breakdown.
Eco-socialists hold that private, profit-seeking ownership of big firms is incompatible with living within ecological limits.
Eco-socialism rejects letting prices and competition alone decide production, because markets ignore planetary limits.
Every major African socialist programme (Nyerere, Nkrumah, Senghor, Kaunda) used national planning to set development priorities, not markets alone.
African socialism appeals to a classless, communal 'familyhood' in which nobody exploits others, so it rejects large wealth gaps.
Social democracy is committed to parliamentary democracy with competing parties.
Social democrats pursue reform through free elections, which requires free party formation and competition.
Social democracy is defined by democratic regulation and correction of markets, not leaving production to prices alone.
Redistribution from concentrated wealth through progressive taxes and the welfare state is central to social democracy.
Progressive liberalism takes liberal democracy, with free party competition, as its framework.
Progressive liberals defend equal voting rights and oppose barriers to voting access.
Equal marriage rights for same-sex couples are a defining equal-rights position of present-day progressive liberalism.
Progressive liberalism's commitment to gender equality rules out giving husbands authority over wives.
The Green pillar of grassroots democracy is incompatible with one-party rule.
Green parties are committed to pluralist, participatory democracy with open electoral competition.
Green politics holds that markets left alone overshoot ecological limits, so production must be regulated.
Non-violence is one of the four Green pillars, so armed force for interests without an attack contradicts it.
Left populism puts popular sovereignty above unelected technocrats and experts.
Left populism is built on taking from the wealthy few to benefit the many.
Left populism defines itself against an oligarchy whose wealth sets it far apart from the people.
Social liberalism requires constitutionally limited, pluralist liberal democracy.
Free political association and electoral competition are basic liberal rights for social liberals.
Social liberalism keeps a mainly private, market-coordinated economy and rejects wholesale collectivisation.
Social liberalism's equal individual liberty excludes legal or normative authority of husbands over wives.
Centrism supports liberal democracy with checks and balances, which excludes one-party rule.
Centrists accept competitive elections as the basis of legitimate government.
Centrism distrusts concentrated power and requires checks and balances, so it would not let a single leader bypass the legislature.
Centrists back a regulated market economy, and nearly total common ownership is an ideological extreme they reject.
The Third Way works within modernised representative democracy and party competition.
Third Way politics assumes open electoral competition among parties.
The Third Way explicitly abandoned old-style state socialism and collective ownership.
The Third Way embraces markets and rejects central planning of production.
Neoliberalism rests on private property and privatisation, the opposite of common ownership.
Neoliberalism holds that markets coordinate dispersed knowledge better than any planner.
Free trade without protectionist barriers is a defining neoliberal policy.
Neoliberals want capital allocated by expected returns in competitive markets, not by planners' goals.
Liberal conservatives treat constitutional, parliamentary democracy as an inherited good to protect.
Liberal conservatism defends competitive liberal democracy, including the freedom to form opposition parties.
Liberal conservatism's commitment to free enterprise and private property rules out common ownership of nearly all assets.
Liberal conservatism rejects state-led economics in favour of free markets.
Burkean conservatism treats private property as a bulwark of independence and continuity, so it rejects wholesale collectivisation.
Burkean conservatism opposes abstract rationalist schemes, and a deliberate plan for the whole economy is one.
Opposing mass immigration to preserve national and cultural continuity is a defining paleoconservative position.
Paleoconservatism defends national sovereignty and decentralised self-government against any world government.
Paleoconservatives reject putting international courts above their own nation's courts and constitution.
Paleoconservatives defend private and family property against collectivist ownership.
Communitarianism, as defined here, keeps democratic institutions and active civic participation, which one-party rule excludes.
Communitarians work within pluralist democracy, where citizens may organise politically to replace those in power.
Christian democracy is committed to constitutional, multiparty democracy.
Christian democratic parties compete in, and defend, free elections.
Christian social teaching defends private property with a social obligation, and rejects collectivist socialism.
Christian democracy favours a social market economy over central planning.
Integralism subordinates temporal power to the Church's spiritual authority, so strict separation contradicts it.
Integralism orders law toward humanity's supernatural end and rejects purely secular grounds for law.
Integralism holds that the state should recognise the true religion, which here is Catholicism.
Integralism takes Catholic teaching on marriage as binding for public law, and that teaching excludes same-sex marriage.
Islamic democracy is defined by elected, accountable government in contrast to autocracy.
Islamic democrats hold that the community chooses its rulers and must be able to replace them through elections.
Islamic democracy holds that Islamic ethical principles should be a source of law, not secular reasons alone.
Theocratic absolutism fuses public authority with religious authority.
Rule by religious authorities who administer sacred law is the defining feature of theocratic absolutism.
Theocratic absolutism holds that law is revealed, not grounded in secular reasons.
In theocratic absolutism, the supreme religious ruler's authority is final and cannot be challenged through elections or parties.
Distributism exists to spread productive property widely and opposes its concentration among a few.
Distributism rejects state socialism and central planning as forms of the 'servile state'.
Ahimsa (non-violence) rules out using armed force abroad when no attack has occurred.
Gandhian non-violence rejects pre-emptive military strikes.
Sarvodaya's ideal relies on unarmed peace brigades and non-violent resistance, not powerful armed forces.
Gram swaraj means self-governing village republics, with law made from below rather than by the centre.
National conservatism is defined by putting the nation ahead of any global community, so ranking loyalty to humanity above one's country rejects its starting premise.
Every variant treats independent nation-states as the proper order of the world, which a binding world government abolishes.
National conservatives across variants hold that sovereign national institutions, not international courts, have the final say.
A cohesive nation that controls its own borders is central to the doctrine, so a universal right to settle in any country contradicts it.
Right populism sets the will of ordinary people against expert and elite judgement, so siding with experts over voters abandons its core claim.
Handing contested questions to an unelected council of the wise is the elite rule that populism exists to oppose.
Reclaiming national sovereignty from supranational bodies is shared by all right-populist movements, so a binding world government contradicts it.
Every right-populist variant demands border control, which a universal right to settle anywhere rules out.
Civic nationalism makes the citizen nation the primary object of political loyalty, so ranking humanity first denies the nationalism in it.
Civic nationalists hold that the nation-state is the main seat of political authority, which a world government with binding laws replaces.
Fascism's ideal state has a single party and leader, so rejecting one-party rule rejects the fascist state form.
Fascism holds that rival parties are obsolete and divisive, so freely competing parties that can replace the rulers contradict it.
Fascism makes the nation the supreme loyalty, so putting humanity ahead of one's country contradicts its core.
Fascism treats national sovereignty as absolute and scorns international bodies, so a binding world government contradicts it.
Republicanism is the first of Kemalism's Six Arrows, and Kemalism abolished the sultanate, so a ruling hereditary monarch contradicts it.
Laiklik keeps religion out of law and politics, so a formal law-making role for clerics contradicts it.
Kemalism replaced religious law with secular law, so basing law on religious authority contradicts its secularism.
Kemalists removed Islam's status as state religion in 1928, and laiklik bars an official religion.
Peronism defines itself as a Third Position against liberal capitalism, with the state directing development, so leaving production to prices and competition alone contradicts it.
Political sovereignty and the nation are among Peronism's three banners, so putting loyalty to humanity above the nation contradicts it.
Peronism's commitment to political sovereignty and non-alignment rules out a world government with binding laws.
Classical liberalism rests on private property and voluntary exchange, so owning nearly all productive assets in common contradicts it.
Every classical-liberal variant holds that productive property is properly private.
Classical liberals hold that markets, not planners, should coordinate the economy.
Constitutionally limited, checked government by consent excludes permanent rule by one party without rivals.
Minarchism holds that property is fully private and that the state only protects rights, so common ownership of productive assets contradicts it.
Minarchists confine the state to police, courts and defence, which rules out the state planning production.
Under self-ownership a person may harm only themselves, so making such drug possession a crime breaches the core principle.
The night-watchman state does not redistribute wealth, so taking from the rich to share with the rest contradicts its limits.
Georgists treat free trade as a core commitment, following George's attack on protection, so taxing imports contradicts it.
Tariffs are a tax on trade, which Georgism holds should be replaced by a single tax on land.
Georgism captures land rent publicly but leaves the economy to markets, so a central production plan contradicts it.
Paleolibertarians hold property rights to be absolute, which common ownership of productive assets abolishes.
Paleolibertarians regard state redistribution of wealth as plunder by the central state.
Paleolibertarians want smaller, decentralised political units and reject global governance outright.
Decentralisation, states' rights and secession are defining paleolibertarian positions, so making most law nationally contradicts them.
Anarcho-communism's ideal holds everything in common, so private ownership of productive assets contradicts it.
Abolishing capital and private ownership of the means of production is the communist part of the doctrine.
Anarchists reject any state or ruling party, including a 'workers' state', so one-party rule contradicts them.
Anarcho-communism replaces markets and money with distribution according to need, so price-and-competition allocation contradicts it.
In the syndicalist ideal, workers' collectives hold productive property in common.
Anarcho-syndicalism aims to take the means of production from private owners and give them to the workers, so private ownership contradicts its goal.
Workers running industry through their syndicates is the defining aim, so large companies must not stay in private hands.
Syndicalists reject parties and the state altogether, so permanent rule by one party contradicts them.
Mutualism rejects absentee ownership that earns without working, which is what ownership by private shareholders is.
Mutualists hold that markets, not planning, should coordinate production in a free society of producers.
As an anarchist doctrine, mutualism replaces authority with contract and voluntary federation, so rule by one party contradicts it.
Libertarian municipalism's ideal puts land and enterprises under municipal ownership, held by the community.
Libertarian municipalism rejects private ownership of productive property in favour of community ownership.
Its confederal design gives higher councils only the powers that local assemblies delegate.
Direct democracy in citizen assemblies is incompatible with one party ruling without rivals.
Anarcho-capitalism holds that all property is private, so common ownership of productive assets contradicts it.
Private ownership of everything, including what states now provide, is the doctrine's foundation.
Anarcho-capitalists regard taxation as theft, so forced redistribution of wealth contradicts the non-aggression principle.
Anarcho-capitalists hold that free markets should coordinate everything, so planned production contradicts the doctrine.
Anarcho-primitivism rejects technological civilisation as a system, so pursuing superhuman AI contradicts it.
Anarcho-primitivists oppose life extension as part of the technological project they want to dismantle.
Anarcho-primitivists oppose genetic engineering, especially enhancement, as domination of nature.
Stateless bands without rulers rule out any party governing a country.
A hereditary sovereign holding real, undivided power is what absolute monarchism means.
Absolute monarchy rejects party politics and any electoral mechanism to replace the sovereign's government.
Absolute monarchists hold that the monarch is not chosen by voters, so citizens electing who governs contradicts the doctrine.
Constitutional monarchism places governing power in an elected parliament, which requires parties that can compete to replace the government.
A monarch above party politics, with power in an elected and accountable parliament, is incompatible with one-party rule.
Technocracy is defined by giving qualified experts' judgement priority over popular opinion.
Technocrats ground authority in scientific competence and evidence, which excludes giving religious leaders a formal law-making role.
Confucian meritocracy holds that officials selected for virtue and ability should decide, not popular opinion, so giving voters priority over the qualified contradicts it.
The developmental state's defining feature is steering investment toward national goals.
Letting investment follow returns alone abandons the state-guided industrial policy that defines the model.
Developmental authoritarians reject unrestricted markets in favour of state-directed development priorities.
Neoreaction rejects democracy, so ruling by citizens' equal votes contradicts it.
In the neoreactionary ideal, a sovereign CEO answers to owners rather than to electoral competitors, so parties that can replace the rulers contradict it.
The neoreactionary ideal is a patchwork of competing sovereign states that people can leave, which a single world government abolishes.
Overcoming ageing through technology is a central transhumanist goal.
Treating ageing as a natural limit not to be cured is the bioconservative position that transhumanism exists to oppose.
Transhumanists reject any absolute ban on heritable genetic modification, whatever its purpose.
Brain-computer interfaces for enhancement, once shown to be safe, fall within the morphological freedom that all transhumanists endorse.
